beats.narration: Begin by framing Introduction to Co-op and Course Purpose as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. This seminar helps students prepare for Computer Science co-operative education employment ("co-op") by developing job search strategies and materials, and reviewing relevant policies. Consider this worked case: A second-year COMPSCI-BS student must complete this course before applying for a summer co-op position. On screen, display a simple flowchart showing 'CS Undergraduate' -> 'CSCI-99 Completion' -> 'Co-op Registration'. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

beats.narration: Now define Prerequisites and Eligibility precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. The seminar will also review various curricular options and program requirements for CS undergraduate students. Consider this worked case: A first-year student cannot enroll until they have completed their introductory computer science courses. On screen, show a checklist graphic with three boxes: 'Major: COMPSCI-BS or COMPEX-UND', 'Standing: 2nd Year or Higher', 'Status: Enrolled'. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.

Completion of this seminar and the related assignments are required before a CS student can be registered for co-op. Consider this worked case: Students attend one 50-minute lecture session each semester to cover orientation and policy reviews. On screen, insert a calendar icon with two highlighted months: 'Fall' and 'Spring', alongside a clock icon labeled '1 Contact Hour'. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Co-op Preparation and Job Search and make the decision criteria explicit. Students are introduced to RIT's Office of Career Services and Cooperative Education, and learn about professional, legal, and ethical responsibilities for their co-op and subsequent professional experiences. Consider this worked case: Students draft a targeted resume and practice technical interview responses using industry-standard co-op application formats. On screen, show a split-screen graphic: left side displays a resume template, right side shows a mock interview checklist. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

beats.narration: Apply Career Services and Cooperative Education Overview to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. They should respect privacy. Consider this worked case: Students learn how to access career counseling, co-op placement portals, and alumni networking resources. On screen, display a directory-style layout with icons for 'Career Counseling', 'Co-op Portal', and 'Alumni Network' under a central 'Office of Career Services' header. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Professional, Legal, and Ethical Responsibilities, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Consider this worked case: Students review confidentiality agreements and data handling protocols required by co-op employers. On screen, show a shield icon divided into three sections labeled 'Professional', 'Legal', and 'Ethical', with brief bullet points underneath each. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around ACM Code of Ethics Foundations with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Computing professionals should avoid harm. Consider this worked case: Students analyze a case study where a developer must choose between meeting a tight deadline and implementing robust security measures. On screen, display a circular diagram with arrows connecting 'Contribute to Society', 'Avoid Harm', 'Maintain High Standards', and 'Ethical Practice' to a central 'ACM Code' node. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a circular diagram with arrows connecting 'Contribute to Society', 'Avoid Harm', 'Maintain High Standards', and 'Ethical Practice' to a central 'ACM Code' node.

beats.narration: Use Ethical Decision-Making Framework to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations. Consider this worked case: Students map out a stakeholder impact chart for a proposed algorithm that processes user data, noting potential privacy risks and mitigation steps. On screen, show a flowchart starting with 'Identify Stakeholders' -> 'Assess Benefits/Harms' -> 'Evaluate Alternatives' -> 'Determine Obligations' -> 'Make Decision'. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart starting with 'Identify Stakeholders' -> 'Assess Benefits/Harms' -> 'Evaluate Alternatives' -> 'Determine Obligations' -> 'Make Decision'.

beats.narration: Connect Responsible Technical Communication to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. Consider this worked case: Students practice rewriting a draft abstract to separate empirical findings from theoretical hypotheses and add proper citations. On screen, display a side-by-side comparison: 'Before' shows a paragraph mixing claims and evidence; 'After' shows clearly separated sections with citation markers. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Responsible Technical Communication
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a side-by-side comparison: 'Before' shows a paragraph mixing claims and evidence; 'After' shows clearly separated sections with citation markers.

beats.narration: Finish with Research Integrity and Methodology as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Consider this worked case: Students draft a methodology section that explicitly states sample sizes, tools used, and known constraints of their experimental setup. On screen, show a checklist graphic with items: 'Methods Described for Evaluation', 'Limitations Disclosed', 'Plagiarism Avoided', 'Conflicts Disclosed'. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist graphic with items: 'Methods Described for Evaluation', 'Limitations Disclosed', 'Plagiarism Avoided', 'Conflicts Disclosed'.

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.
sources.title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.
